ii-a: Introduction to Securities
Which of the following best describes the role of the primary market?
It is the market in which derivatives on listed shares are settled
It is the market where only the RBI deals in government bonds
It is where investors trade already-listed securities among themselves
It is where issuers raise fresh capital by selling newly issued securities to investors
New securities are created and sold by issuers in the primary market; trading of existing securities happens in the secondary market.
Introduction to Securities
An investor who holds a company's debentures is best described as the company's:
Owner
Registrar
Creditor
Promoter
Debentures are debt instruments, so holders lend money to the company and are its creditors, not its owners.
Introduction to Securities
Which body is the principal regulator of the Indian securities market?
Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Reserve Bank of India
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
Securities and Exchange Board of India
SEBI was set up to protect investors and to develop and regulate the securities market.
Characteristics of Equity Shares
In the event of liquidation, equity shareholders are paid:
Only after all creditors and preference shareholders have been paid
Pari passu with debenture holders
Before preference shareholders but after creditors
Before secured creditors
Equity holders carry residual risk and receive whatever remains after all prior claims are settled.
Characteristics of Equity Shares
A shareholder holds 300 shares when a company announces a 1:2 bonus issue (one bonus share for every two held). How many shares will the shareholder hold after the bonus?
One bonus share for every two held gives 300 ÷ 2 = 150 bonus shares, so the total becomes 300 + 150 = 450.
Characteristics of Equity Shares
A company splits its shares from a face value of ₹10 to ₹2 each. An investor holding 100 shares will now hold:
200 shares of ₹5 each
500 shares of ₹2 each
20 shares of ₹10 each
100 shares of ₹2 each
A split divides each ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares, so 100 shares become 500 while the total face value stays the same.
Characteristics of Equity Shares
Which corporate action reduces the number of a company's outstanding shares by purchasing them back from shareholders?
Bonus issue
Rights issue
Stock split
Buyback
In a buyback the company buys its own shares and extinguishes them, so fewer shares remain outstanding.
Characteristics of Debt Securities
A bond with a face value of ₹1,000 carries a coupon of 8% per annum payable annually. What is the annual interest received?
Coupon is calculated on face value: 8% of ₹1,000 = ₹80 per year.
Characteristics of Debt Securities
A zero-coupon bond provides a return to the investor because it is:
Issued at face value and pays a floating coupon
Issued at a discount and redeemed at face value
Converted into equity at maturity
Redeemed at a value below its issue price
Zero-coupon bonds pay no periodic interest; the gap between the discounted issue price and the face value is the investor's return.
Characteristics of Debt Securities
When market interest rates rise, the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond generally:
Rises
Becomes equal to its face value
Falls
Stays unchanged
Bond prices move inversely to yields, since the fixed coupon becomes less attractive compared with new issues.
Characteristics of Other Securities
A warrant attached to a security gives the holder:
A fixed coupon payable every quarter
Voting rights immediately on issue
The right, but not the obligation, to acquire shares at a specified price within a set period
An obligation to buy shares at market price
A warrant is an option-like right to subscribe to shares at a pre-set price; the holder may choose not to exercise it.
Characteristics of Other Securities
A Global Depository Receipt (GDR) issued by an Indian company represents:
Units of an Indian mutual fund sold abroad
A rupee bond issued in India by a foreign company
Shares of a foreign company listed on Indian exchanges
Underlying shares of the Indian company held by a domestic custodian, with the receipts traded overseas
Depository receipts let foreign investors hold claims on Indian shares that are held in custody in India.
Characteristics of Other Securities
Which instrument lets a foreign company raise capital from Indian investors by listing receipts on Indian stock exchanges?
Global Depository Receipt
American Depository Receipt
Indian Depository Receipt
Foreign Currency Convertible Bond
An IDR represents shares of a foreign company and is issued and listed in India.
Basics of Mutual Funds
The Net Asset Value (NAV) of a mutual fund scheme per unit is computed as:
(Assets + liabilities) ÷ units outstanding
Total income ÷ number of unitholders
Total assets ÷ face value of units
(Market value of assets − liabilities) ÷ number of units outstanding
NAV per unit is the scheme's net assets divided by units outstanding.
Basics of Mutual Funds
In which type of scheme can investors buy and redeem units from the fund on any business day at NAV-linked prices?
Fixed maturity plan after listing
Interval scheme only during its NFO
Open-ended scheme
Close-ended scheme
Open-ended schemes offer continuous sale and repurchase of units.
SEBI – Role and Regulations
SEBI received statutory powers under which legislation?
SEBI Act, 1992
Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956
Depositories Act, 1996
Companies Act, 1956
SEBI was set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body and became a statutory regulator under the SEBI Act, 1992.
SEBI – Role and Regulations
An RTA wants to begin acting as a Registrar to an Issue. What must it obtain first?
A certificate of registration from SEBI
A banking licence from the RBI
Approval from the stock exchange where the issuer is listed
A licence from the Registrar of Companies
Registrars and share transfer agents are SEBI intermediaries and must be registered with SEBI before acting as such.
SEBI – Role and Regulations
An intermediary aggrieved by a SEBI order can file an appeal with:
Securities Appellate Tribunal
National Company Law Tribunal
Ministry of Finance
Reserve Bank of India
Appeals against SEBI orders lie before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT).
Public Offer of Securities
In a book-built issue, the price at which shares are finally allotted is called the:
Floor price
Cut-off price
Reserve price
Face value
Book building discovers the price from bids within the band; allotment is made at the discovered cut-off price.
Public Offer of Securities
An IPO has a price band of ₹190–₹200 and a lot size of 75 shares. What is the maximum number of lots a retail individual investor can bid for at the upper end without exceeding ₹2 lakh?
13 lots
10 lots
14 lots
26 lots
Each lot costs 75 × ₹200 = ₹15,000; 13 lots = ₹1,95,000, while 14 lots = ₹2,10,000 would exceed the ₹2 lakh retail limit.
Public Offer of Securities
What distinguishes an offer for sale (OFS) component in an IPO from a fresh issue?
An OFS can only be made to qualified institutional buyers
In an OFS the company issues new shares to the public
In an OFS existing shareholders sell their shares, so the proceeds go to them and not to the company
An OFS always increases the company's paid-up capital
An OFS transfers existing shares; the company's capital does not increase and the selling shareholders receive the money.
Public Offer of Securities
A green shoe option in a public issue is used mainly to:
Refund excess application money faster
Stabilise the post-listing price through an over-allotment mechanism
Convert debt into equity at listing
Allot shares at a discount to employees
The stabilising agent uses over-allotted shares to support the price if it falls below the issue price after listing.
Public Offer of Securities
A retail individual investor in a public issue is one who applies for securities worth:
Not more than ₹5 lakh
Not more than ₹10 lakh
Not more than ₹50,000
Not more than ₹2 lakh
Under SEBI ICDR, a retail individual investor bids for up to ₹2 lakh in an issue.
Modes of Allotment other than Public Offers
A shareholder holds 800 shares and the company announces a rights issue in the ratio 1:4. How many rights shares is the shareholder entitled to?
A 1:4 ratio means one new share for every four held: 800 ÷ 4 = 200.
Modes of Allotment other than Public Offers
Rights entitlements in a rights issue are credited to eligible shareholders:
In dematerialised form, and they can be renounced or traded on the exchange during the renunciation period
Only to promoters
To the RTA's own account until the issue closes
Only as physical letters of offer that cannot be transferred
Rights entitlements are credited in demat form and can be renounced on-market or off-market before the issue closes.
Modes of Allotment other than Public Offers
Allotment of shares by a listed company only to qualified institutional buyers, without a public offer document, is known as:
Qualified Institutions Placement
Employee stock option scheme
Bonus issue
Rights issue
A QIP lets listed companies raise capital quickly from QIBs only.
Modes of Allotment other than Public Offers
Allotment of shares to a select group of identified persons, such as a strategic investor, by a listed company is called:
Public issue
Preferential allotment
Offer for sale
Sweat equity
A preferential issue is made to specified persons on a private basis, subject to SEBI ICDR conditions.
Processes related to Public Offering of Shares
Under ASBA, the investor's application money is:
Paid by cheque to the registrar
Blocked in the investor's bank account and debited only on allotment
Deposited with the stock exchange
Transferred upfront to the issuer's account
ASBA keeps funds in the investor's account until the basis of allotment is finalised; only the allotted amount is debited.
Processes related to Public Offering of Shares
Within how many working days after an issue closes must the shares be listed under SEBI's current public issue timeline?
T+12 working days
T+3 working days
T+6 working days
T+1 working day
SEBI has made the T+3 listing timeline mandatory for public issues, where T is the issue closing date.
Processes related to Public Offering of Shares
Individual investors can use the UPI mechanism to apply in a public issue for amounts up to:
₹5 lakh
₹10 lakh
₹2 lakh
₹1 lakh
SEBI raised the UPI limit for individual bidders in public issues to ₹5 lakh.
Processes related to Public Offering of Shares
In an oversubscribed issue, which entity finalises the basis of allotment in consultation with the designated stock exchange?
The sponsor bank alone
The Registrar to the Issue, together with the issuer and lead manager
SEBI
The depository participant of each investor
The registrar processes the bids and finalises the basis of allotment with the designated stock exchange, issuer and lead managers.
Roles and Responsibilities in a Public Issue
Which intermediary is responsible for due diligence of the offer document and managing the overall issue process?
Depository participant
Lead manager (merchant banker)
Self-Certified Syndicate Bank
Registrar to the Issue
The book-running lead manager is a SEBI-registered merchant banker who handles due diligence and manages the issue.
Roles and Responsibilities in a Public Issue
In a UPI-based IPO application, the bank that acts as a conduit between the stock exchanges and the NPCI to block and unblock funds is the:
Escrow collection bank
Banker to the issue for refunds only
Clearing bank
Sponsor bank
The sponsor bank, appointed by the issuer, initiates UPI mandate requests and processes block and unblock instructions.
Roles and Responsibilities in a Public Issue
Which entity is a bank registered with SEBI to accept ASBA applications and block funds in investors' accounts?
Self-Certified Syndicate Bank
Credit rating agency
Debenture trustee
Clearing corporation
SCSBs are banks registered with SEBI to offer ASBA services.
Roles and Responsibilities in a Public Issue
After allotment is finalised, which activity is typically carried out by the Registrar to the Issue?
Rating the shares being issued
Fixing the price band
Underwriting any unsubscribed portion
Arranging credit of allotted shares to investors' demat accounts through the depositories
The registrar sends allotment details to the depositories for crediting shares and coordinates unblocking of funds.
Depository Services
In the depository system, who is the registered owner of the dematerialised securities in the company's records?
The depository participant
The RTA
The stock exchange
The depository
Under the Depositories Act, 1996, the depository is the registered owner, while the investor is the beneficial owner.
Depository Services
The two depositories operating in India are:
CAMS and KFintech
NSCCL and ICCL
NSE and BSE
NSDL and CDSL
National Securities Depository Ltd and Central Depository Services (India) Ltd are India's depositories.
Depository Services
An ISIN allotted to an Indian security is a code made up of:
8 characters beginning with 'ISN'
16 digits linked to the stock exchange code
12 alphanumeric characters beginning with 'IN'
10 digits beginning with the company's PAN
An ISIN is a 12-character code, and Indian securities begin with the country code 'IN'.
Processes related to Depositories
An investor submits a demat request form with share certificates to the DP. What does the DP do next?
Sends an electronic request to the depository and forwards the physical certificates to the issuer's RTA
Returns the certificates to the investor after scanning
Credits the shares immediately without waiting for verification
Sends the certificates to SEBI for cancellation
The DP raises an electronic request and sends the certificates to the RTA, which verifies them and confirms the demat request to the depository.
Processes related to Depositories
Converting dematerialised holdings back into physical certificates is called:
Rematerialisation
Transmission
Consolidation
Transposition
Remat is the reverse of demat; the RTA prints certificates after the depository confirms the request.
Processes related to Depositories
Before sending share certificates for dematerialisation, the investor should:
Get them attested by a notary
Submit them to the stock exchange
Deface them by marking 'Surrendered for Dematerialisation'
Endorse them in favour of the DP
Defacing the certificates prevents misuse while they are in transit to the RTA.
Processes related to Depositories
When a company credits bonus shares to shareholders holding in demat form, the RTA uses:
The list of brokers registered with the exchange
The list of applicants in the company's last IPO
The list of beneficial owners as on the record date provided by the depositories
Investors' latest income tax returns
Corporate action entitlements for demat holders are based on the beneficial-owner positions downloaded from the depositories as on the record date.
Investor Interface with the R&T Agent
A holder of physical shares wants to change the order of names of joint holders. This request is known as:
Sub-division
Transposition
Transfer
Transmission
Transposition changes the sequence of joint holders' names without changing ownership.
Investor Interface with the R&T Agent
On the death of a sole shareholder with a registered nominee, the shares are passed to the nominee through:
Transmission
Forfeiture
Transfer by sale
Transposition
Transmission is the transfer of securities by operation of law on death, insolvency or similar events.
Investor Interface with the R&T Agent
When an RTA processes a service request for physical securities, such as issuing duplicate certificates, current SEBI norms require it to issue:
A bonus share certificate
A refund of the share value
A Letter of Confirmation, which the investor uses to get the securities dematerialised
A fresh physical share certificate
SEBI requires RTAs to issue a Letter of Confirmation instead of physical certificates for such requests, so that the securities move into demat.
Investor Interface with the R&T Agent
Since April 2019, can a transfer of shares of a listed company be processed in physical form?
Yes, but only if the transfer is between relatives
No; transfers must be in dematerialised form, although transmission and transposition requests for physical shares are allowed
Yes, any transfer can be processed in physical form
No, and physical shares can no longer be dematerialised either
SEBI stopped physical transfers of listed securities, though holders can still dematerialise and use transmission or transposition.
Secondary Market Transactions
Under the standard rolling settlement cycle for equity in India, an investor who buys shares on a Tuesday (with no holidays) receives them on:
Thursday
Tuesday itself
Wednesday
Friday
Indian equity markets follow T+1 settlement, so a Tuesday trade settles on Wednesday.
Secondary Market Transactions
Which entity guarantees settlement of trades executed on a stock exchange?
The issuer company
The investor's bank
The clearing corporation
The RTA of the company
The clearing corporation acts as central counterparty and guarantees settlement of exchange trades.
Client Servicing
An investor whose complaint against a listed company's RTA is not resolved can lodge it online with SEBI through:
MCA21
e-filing portal of the Income Tax Department
NPCI portal
SCORES
SCORES is SEBI's online grievance redressal platform for securities market complaints.
Client Servicing
A good practice for an RTA receiving an investor's written request is to:
Act only if the request comes through the company's directors
Acknowledge it, log it in the inward register and act within the prescribed time
Forward it to SEBI for action
Act only after the investor sends three reminders
Recording and acknowledging requests and acting within timelines is central to RTA client servicing.
ii-b: Introduction to Securities
Which of the following is a money market instrument?
Treasury bill
Equity share
Ten-year government bond
Convertible debenture
T-bills are short-term government securities with maturities under one year, which makes them money market instruments.
Introduction to Securities
The secondary market primarily provides investors with:
Guaranteed returns
Tax-free income
Liquidity, by allowing them to sell existing securities to other investors
Fresh capital for issuers
Trading among investors in the secondary market lets holders exit their investments.
Characteristics of Equity Shares
Which of the following is a right typically enjoyed by equity shareholders?
Repayment of capital on a fixed maturity date
Priority over creditors on liquidation
A fixed rate of dividend every year
Voting on resolutions at general meetings
Equity shareholders own the company and vote; dividends are not fixed and they rank last on liquidation.
Characteristics of Equity Shares
Dividend on equity shares is paid:
Only on liquidation
As a fixed percentage of face value every year
At the discretion of the company out of its profits
Even when the company has no profits or reserves
Equity dividend is not a contractual obligation; the board recommends it based on profits.
Characteristics of Debt Securities
Credit risk in a debt security refers to the risk that:
Inflation may erode real returns
The security may not be easy to sell
The issuer may fail to pay interest or principal on time
Interest rates in the market may rise
Credit (default) risk is about the issuer's ability to meet payment obligations.
Characteristics of Debt Securities
A bond whose coupon is reset periodically with reference to a benchmark rate is called a:
Perpetual bond
Zero-coupon bond
Fixed rate bond
Floating rate bond
Floating rate bonds pay a coupon linked to a benchmark, so it changes at each reset.
Characteristics of Other Securities
A security with features of both debt and equity, such as a convertible debenture, is described as a:
Pure equity instrument
Derivative
Money market instrument
Hybrid instrument
Convertibles start as debt and may convert into equity, so they combine features of both.
Characteristics of Other Securities
Which of the following is a derivative instrument?
Commercial paper
Equity share
Index futures contract
Treasury bill
A futures contract derives its value from an underlying, such as an index.
SEBI – Role and Regulations
Mutual funds in India are regulated by SEBI under the:
Insurance Act, 1938
SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
Banking Regulation Act, 1949
SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020
SEBI regulates mutual funds through the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996.
SEBI – Role and Regulations
Which of the following is NOT a function of SEBI?
Setting the repo rate
Registering and regulating market intermediaries
Prohibiting insider trading
Promoting investor education
The repo rate is set by the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee; the other three are SEBI functions.
SEBI – Role and Regulations
SEBI's online platform for investors to lodge complaints against mutual funds and RTAs is:
CERSAI
NACH
SCORES
MF Central
SCORES is SEBI's complaints redress system.
Basics of Registrars and Transfer Agents
In the mutual fund industry, an RTA is appointed by:
AMFI
The custodian
The Asset Management Company, on behalf of the mutual fund
The investor
The AMC appoints the RTA to maintain unitholder records and process transactions for the fund's schemes.
Basics of Registrars and Transfer Agents
Which of the following is a typical function of a mutual fund RTA?
Managing the scheme's investment portfolio
Holding the scheme's securities in safe custody
Setting the scheme's investment objective
Processing purchase, redemption and switch requests and maintaining unitholder records
RTAs handle investor servicing and records, while the fund manager invests and the custodian holds the assets.
Basics of Registrars and Transfer Agents
A folio number in a mutual fund is:
The scheme's code on the stock exchange
The investor's PAN
A unique account number given to an investor in the fund's records
The scheme's SEBI registration number
A folio identifies an investor's account with the fund house, and many schemes can be held under one folio.
Basics of Registrars and Transfer Agents
An investor visits an RTA service centre to submit a redemption request for an open-ended scheme. Which role is the RTA performing here?
Acting as the scheme's auditor
Acting as an official point of acceptance of transactions
Acting as the fund manager
Acting as the trustee
RTA offices serve as official points of acceptance where transactions are time-stamped for NAV applicability.
Registrar and Transfer Agents Regulations
Under the SEBI (Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents) Regulations, 1993, a Category I registrant may act as:
Only a share transfer agent
A merchant banker and registrar
Only a registrar to an issue
Both registrar to an issue and share transfer agent
Category I covers both activities, while Category II permits only one of the two.
Registrar and Transfer Agents Regulations
An RTA discovers that one of its employees has been sharing unitholders' contact data with an outside marketing firm. This most directly breaches the RTA's obligation to:
Underwrite NFOs
Maintain confidentiality of investor records under its code of conduct
Publish daily NAVs
Achieve minimum transaction volumes
The code of conduct for RTAs requires them to protect investor information and avoid misuse.
Registrar and Transfer Agents Regulations
Which of the following must an RTA do under SEBI regulations?
Approve the AMC's investment decisions
Maintain proper books and records and make them available for SEBI inspection
Invest its own funds in the schemes it services
Guarantee investors' returns
Registered RTAs must maintain records for the prescribed period and are subject to SEBI inspection.
Basics of Mutual Funds
A key benefit of investing through a mutual fund is:
Freedom from all market risk
Direct voting rights in every portfolio company
Diversification and professional management even with a small investment
Guaranteed returns on all schemes
Pooling lets small investors get a diversified, professionally managed portfolio; returns are not guaranteed.
Basics of Mutual Funds
A scheme has assets with a market value of ₹102 crore, liabilities of ₹2 crore and 5 crore units outstanding. What is its NAV per unit?
NAV = (102 − 2) ÷ 5 = ₹20 per unit.
Basics of Mutual Funds
Which of these is an example of a close-ended scheme feature?
Units can be bought and redeemed on any business day
There is no maturity date and units are issued continuously
Units are created daily through SIPs
Units can be bought only during the NFO and the scheme has a fixed maturity
Close-ended schemes sell units only in the NFO, have a fixed tenure and are listed to provide liquidity.
Mutual Fund Structure and Constituents
In India, a mutual fund is constituted as a:
Trust
Co-operative society
Private limited company
Partnership firm
Mutual funds are set up as trusts under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, with the sponsor as settlor.
Mutual Fund Structure and Constituents
Under SEBI regulations, the sponsor of a mutual fund must hold at least what share of the AMC's net worth?
The sponsor must contribute at least 40% of the AMC's net worth.
Mutual Fund Structure and Constituents
Who holds the securities of a mutual fund scheme in safe custody?
The custodian
The RTA
The distributor
The AMC's fund manager
A SEBI-registered custodian holds the fund's securities and handles their settlement.
Mutual Fund Structure and Constituents
Which constituent is primarily responsible for protecting unitholders' interests and supervising the AMC?
The RTA
The trustees
The registrar of companies
The distributors
Trustees hold the property in trust for unitholders and oversee the AMC.
Mutual Fund Products
Which scheme type is eligible for an income tax deduction under the old tax regime and has a statutory lock-in of three years?
Liquid fund
Equity Linked Savings Scheme
Overnight fund
Arbitrage fund
ELSS is the tax-saving equity scheme category; it carries a three-year lock-in and qualifies for deduction only under the old tax regime.
Mutual Fund Products
An overnight fund invests in securities with a maturity of:
One day
Three to six months
Up to 91 days
More than seven years
SEBI's categorisation defines overnight funds as investing in overnight securities with one-day maturity.
Mutual Fund Products
An index fund aims to:
Guarantee capital protection
Invest only in debt
Replicate the performance of a specified index
Beat the index through active stock selection
Index funds are passive and hold the index constituents in the same proportions.
Mutual Fund Products
Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) differ from regular open-ended funds because ETF units:
Are listed and can be traded on stock exchanges at market prices during trading hours
Cannot be held in demat form
Are priced only once a day at closing NAV for all investors
Can only be bought during the NFO
ETF units trade on the exchange throughout the day like shares.
Operational Concepts of Mutual Funds
For a purchase in a liquid fund, the cut-off time to get the same day's closing NAV (with funds realised in time) is:
Liquid and overnight funds have a 1:30 p.m. cut-off for purchases, compared with 3:00 p.m. for most other schemes.
Operational Concepts of Mutual Funds
For purchases in mutual fund schemes, the applicable NAV is determined based on:
The time the funds are realised and available to the scheme, subject to the cut-off time
The date written on the application form
The date of the NFO
The date the investor's cheque is printed
SEBI ties NAV applicability for purchases to when the funds are realised in the scheme's account, irrespective of amount.
Operational Concepts of Mutual Funds
An investor invests ₹1,00,000 in a scheme. After stamp duty of 0.005%, the amount available for allotment is:
Stamp duty = 0.005% × 1,00,000 = ₹5, so ₹99,995 is invested.
Operational Concepts of Mutual Funds
An investor redeems units worth ₹50,000 at NAV, and the scheme charges a 1% exit load. What amount does the investor receive (ignoring taxes)?
Exit load = 1% × 50,000 = ₹500, so ₹49,500 is paid out.
Operational Concepts of Mutual Funds
In a Systematic Withdrawal Plan, the investor:
Moves money from one scheme to another at regular intervals
Redeems a fixed amount or units at regular intervals from a scheme
Reinvests all dividends automatically
Invests a fixed amount at regular intervals
An SWP is periodic redemption; an SIP is periodic investment and an STP is periodic switching.
Investors in Mutual Funds
For a mutual fund folio held in the name of a minor, payment for investments must come from:
The distributor's account
Any third party's bank account
Only the guardian's individual account
A bank account of the minor or a joint account of the minor with the guardian
SEBI requires investments in a minor's folio to be paid from the minor's own account or the minor's joint account with the guardian.
Investors in Mutual Funds
When a minor unitholder becomes a major, the RTA must:
Continue the folio in the guardian's name forever
Process a change of status from minor to major and update KYC and bank details in the new major's name
Transfer the units to the guardian
Close the folio and pay out the units to the guardian
On attaining majority, the folio's status must be changed and the investor's own KYC and bank details recorded.
Investors in Mutual Funds
Who among the following can invest in Indian mutual funds on a repatriable basis?
An Overseas Corporate Body
A Non-Resident Indian investing through an NRE account
Any foreign national resident abroad without restriction
A minor through a third party's account
NRIs can invest on a repatriable basis using NRE accounts, subject to the scheme's terms.
Banking Operations in Mutual Funds
Mutual funds generally do NOT accept which kind of payment for subscriptions?
Payments through a registered bank mandate for SIPs
Cheques from the investor's own account
NEFT from the first holder's bank account
Third-party payments, except in permitted cases
To curb money laundering, SEBI and AMFI norms bar third-party payments except for specified exceptions.
Banking Operations in Mutual Funds
SIP instalments are most commonly collected through:
Auto-debit mandates registered on NACH
Credit card cash advances
Demand drafts sent every month
Cash deposited at the AMC branch
NACH mandates let the scheme debit the investor's bank account automatically on SIP dates.
Banking Operations in Mutual Funds
An investor's SIP cheque bounces because of insufficient funds. The RTA should:
Treat it as a redemption
Reverse the allotment of units made against that instalment
Allot units and recover the money later from the distributor
Close the folio permanently
Units allotted against a dishonoured payment are reversed because the funds were never realised.
Financial Transactions
An investor invests ₹49,997.50 (after stamp duty) in a scheme at an NAV of ₹25. How many units are allotted?
Financial Transactions
A switch from Scheme A to Scheme B of the same fund house is treated as:
A change of bank mandate
A non-financial transaction
A transfer of units without any redemption
A redemption from Scheme A and a purchase in Scheme B
A switch-out is a redemption and a switch-in is a purchase, each at its applicable NAV and charges.
Financial Transactions
Under the current SEBI framework, redemption proceeds for most mutual fund schemes must be transferred to unitholders within:
15 calendar days
30 days
3 working days of the redemption request
10 working days
SEBI and AMFI reduced the redemption payout timeline to 3 working days, with exceptions only for specified scheme types.
Financial Transactions
For an IDCW (dividend) declared by a scheme, payment must be made to unitholders within:
30 days from the record date
15 working days from declaration
7 working days from the record date
One working day
SEBI requires IDCW payouts within 7 working days of the record date.
Financial Transactions
In a Systematic Transfer Plan, the investor:
Periodically switches a fixed amount from one scheme to another scheme of the same fund
Invests a lump sum only once
Transfers units to another investor's folio
Periodically redeems units to their bank account
An STP moves money at intervals between schemes of the same mutual fund, often from a debt fund to an equity fund.
Non-Financial Transactions
Which of the following is a non-financial transaction in a mutual fund folio?
Switch-out
Redemption
SIP instalment
Change of bank mandate
Changes to bank details, address or nominee alter records without moving money.
Non-Financial Transactions
When the sole unitholder of a folio dies and a nominee is registered, the units are passed to the nominee through:
Switch
Transmission
Pledge
Redemption

PAN is the mandatory identifier; other proofs of address and identity can vary.
DP Functions – Account Opening
What is the maximum number of holders permitted in a single demat account?
Five
Three
Two
Four
A demat account can have a first holder and up to two joint holders.
DP Functions – Account Opening
A demat account in the name of a minor:
Can have the minor as a joint holder with parents
Cannot be opened under any circumstance
Is operated by the guardian, and the minor must be the sole holder
Is operated by the minor directly
Minors can only be sole holders, with a guardian operating the account.
DP Functions – Account Opening
Under SEBI's framework, a client who wants the broker to debit securities for settlement and margin pledges can execute a limited-purpose document called:
Letter of Confirmation
Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction (DDPI)
General Power of Attorney with unlimited rights
Delivery Instruction Slip booklet
DDPI replaced the broad PoA for limited purposes such as settlement deliveries and margin pledges.
DP Functions – Account Opening
In-person verification (IPV) of a client opening a demat account:
Is no longer required for any client
Can be done through video-based verification as permitted by SEBI
Is done by the RTA of the company
Must be done only at SEBI's office
SEBI allows video-based IPV (VIPV) as part of KYC.
DP Functions – Account Operations
A client wants to stop all debits from their demat account for some time. The DP can:
Reject the request because freezing is not allowed
Close the account and reopen it later
Transfer holdings to the DP's own account
Freeze the account for debits as per the client's request
Clients can request freezing of debits, credits or both for a period.
DP Functions – Account Operations
An investor wants to add a second holder to an existing sole-holder demat account. The correct approach is to:
Send a request to SEBI
Open a new joint account and transfer the holdings to it
Submit a request to add the name to the existing account
Ask the RTA to change the holder's name
Holders cannot be added or removed in an existing account; a new account is opened and holdings are moved.
DP Functions – Account Operations
A Delivery Instruction Slip (DIS) is used for:
Applying for an IPO
Instructing the DP to debit securities from the account for transfer
Changing the client's address
Requesting dematerialisation
The DIS authorises the DP to debit securities for market or off-market transfers.
DP Functions – Account Operations
A client with holdings wants to close a demat account. The DP will:
Close the account after the client transfers the holdings to another account or rematerialises them
Close it immediately and sell all holdings
Transfer the holdings to the DP's pool account
Refuse closure while holdings exist under any circumstances
Closure requires holdings to be transferred to another demat account or rematerialised.
DP Functions – Account Operations
Transferring shares between an account at NSDL and an account at CDSL is called:
Inter-depository transfer
Rematerialisation
Inter-settlement transfer
Transmission
Transfers across the two depositories are inter-depository transfers.
DP Functions – Transmission and Nomination
A sole holder of a demat account has died and a nominee is registered. To claim the securities, the nominee should submit:
A rematerialisation request
Only a verbal request at the DP office
A DIS signed by the deceased
A transmission request form with a copy of the death certificate and KYC documents
Transmission to a nominee requires the prescribed form, death certificate and the nominee's KYC.
DP Functions – Transmission and Nomination
In a joint demat account, one of the joint holders dies. The securities will be:
Sold by the DP
Transferred to the nominee, ignoring the surviving holders
Transmitted to the surviving joint holders
Frozen permanently
In joint accounts, surviving holders receive the securities on transmission.
DP Functions – Transmission and Nomination
Which of the following cannot make a nomination for a demat account?
A body corporate
Joint individual holders
An individual NRI holder
A sole individual holder
Nomination is available only to individual holders, not to companies or other non-individuals.
DP Functions – Transmission and Nomination
A minor is appointed as nominee in a demat account. On the holder's death, the securities are transmitted to:
The DP
The RTA
The minor, through the guardian named in the nomination
The deceased's employer
A minor can be a nominee; the guardian acts on the minor's behalf.
DP Functions – Dematerialisation
An investor submits a demat request, but the RTA rejects it because the signature does not match its records. The likely next step is to:
Credit the shares anyway
Transfer the shares to the DP
Cancel the shares permanently
Return the certificates to the investor so that the signature can be updated and the request resubmitted
Rejected requests are returned with reasons so the investor can correct the discrepancy.
DP Functions – Dematerialisation
When locked-in shares are dematerialised, they:
Are converted into debentures
Cannot be dematerialised
Remain locked-in in the demat account until the lock-in period ends
Become freely transferable at once
The depository records the lock-in status and allows transfers only after lock-in expires.
DP Functions – Dematerialisation
In the demat process, who confirms the electronic request so that the depository credits the investor's account?
The investor's broker
SEBI
The stock exchange
The issuer's RTA
After verifying the certificates, the RTA confirms the request and the depository credits the account.
DP Functions – Dematerialisation
A remat request results in:
New shares being allotted by the company
Shares being sold on the exchange
Physical certificates being issued by the RTA and the demat balance being debited
Securities moving to another depository
Rematerialisation converts electronic holdings back into physical form.
DP Functions – Trading and Settlement
An investor sells shares on a Thursday under the T+1 cycle (no holidays). By when must the securities reach the clearing corporation for pay-in?
The following Monday
Friday, the settlement day
Thursday evening
The following Tuesday
Pay-in and pay-out of securities happen on T+1, i.e. Friday.
DP Functions – Trading and Settlement
Under the current SEBI framework, after settlement of a buy trade, the securities are generally credited by the clearing corporation:
Directly to the client's demat account
To the exchange's account
To the broker's pool account for an indefinite period
To the RTA's account
SEBI mandated direct payout of securities to client demat accounts to protect client assets.
DP Functions – Trading and Settlement
Which transfer is NOT routed through a stock exchange settlement?
Auction delivery
Pay-out for a purchase on the exchange
Pay-in for a sale on the exchange
Off-market transfer, such as a gift of shares to a family member
Off-market transfers move securities directly between demat accounts without exchange settlement.
DP Functions – Trading and Settlement
For an off-market transfer, depositories require the transferor to specify:
The market price of the securities
The issuer's PAN
The broker's SEBI registration
The reason or purpose of the transfer
Reason codes are required for off-market transfers for monitoring and tax purposes.
Special Services – Pledge & Hypothecation
In a pledge of dematerialised securities, the pledge request is initiated by:
The pledgor (the owner of the securities)
The depository
The pledgee
The RTA
The pledgor initiates the request through their DP, and the pledgee accepts it through theirs.
Special Services – Pledge & Hypothecation
Under the margin pledge mechanism, a client who wants to give shares as margin to the broker:
Sends physical certificates to the broker
Sells the shares and gives cash
Transfers the shares to the broker's own account
Pledges the shares in favour of the broker from their own demat account
Since 2020 margin collateral is provided through pledges, so securities stay in the client's account.
Special Services – Pledge & Hypothecation
If the borrower defaults, the pledgee transfers the pledged securities to itself through:
Rematerialisation
Invocation of the pledge
Closure of the pledge
Transmission
Invocation transfers the pledged securities to the pledgee on default.
Special Services – Public Offering / Corporate Actions
Shares allotted in an IPO are credited to investors' demat accounts by:
The broker, by transferring from its pool
The stock exchange, after listing
SEBI
The RTA, which executes a corporate action through the depositories
The RTA uploads allotment details and the depositories credit investors' accounts.
Special Services – Public Offering / Corporate Actions
For a cash dividend, entitlement is decided based on holdings as on the:
Date of payment
Record date
Date of the AGM notice
Date of IPO allotment
The record date determines which beneficial owners receive the corporate benefit.
Special Services – Public Offering / Corporate Actions
A company announces a 1:1 bonus. An investor holds 250 shares on the record date. How many bonus shares will be credited?
A 1:1 bonus gives one new share for each share held, so 250 shares are credited.
Special Services – Debt Instruments & Government Securities
Commercial paper and certificates of deposit in India are issued:
Only in dematerialised form
Either form at the issuer's choice
Only as bearer certificates
Only in physical form
RBI rules require CPs and CDs to be issued and held in demat form.
Special Services – Debt Instruments & Government Securities
Retail investors holding government securities through a depository account are recorded in the RBI's books through:
The depository's Constituent SGL (gilt) account with the RBI
The clearing bank's current account
The stock exchange's escrow account
The investor's own SGL account automatically
Depositories hold G-Secs for investors through CSGL accounts maintained with the RBI.
Special Services – Debt Instruments & Government Securities
Which of these instruments typically pays no periodic interest and is issued at a discount to its face value?
Treasury bill
Fixed-rate corporate debenture
Perpetual bond
Floating rate bond
T-bills are discount instruments and are redeemed at face value.
Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI)
A foreign pension fund wants to invest in Indian listed shares as an FPI. It obtains registration from:
The RBI directly
The stock exchange
A Designated Depository Participant
The Indian embassy
DDPs grant FPI registration on behalf of SEBI.
Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI)
FPIs generally settle their trades in Indian securities through:
Custodians, who confirm trades and handle settlement
The Ministry of Finance
RTAs
Retail brokers' pool accounts
FPIs appoint custodians who confirm trades and settle them with the clearing corporation.
Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI)
An FPI investor group buys shares of a listed company and its holding reaches 11% of paid-up equity. What happens under the FPI framework?
Nothing; there is no limit
The FPI's registration is cancelled automatically
The investment beyond the limit must be divested or reclassified as FDI within the prescribed time
The shares are cancelled by the company
FPI holdings must stay below 10%; a breach must be cured by divestment or reclassified as FDI.
Investor Services
A DP must send a demat account holder a transaction statement:
Daily
Only once a year
Only on request
Monthly if there are transactions, and otherwise at least quarterly
Depository norms require statements at these minimum frequencies, and they can be sent electronically.
Investor Services
A consolidated account statement covering demat holdings and mutual fund units held in physical (non-demat) form is sent by:
SEBI
The stock exchanges
The depositories
The investor's employer
Depositories send the CAS, combining demat holdings and MF folios linked by PAN.
Investor Services
A demat holder's complaint against a DP is not resolved by the DP. The investor can next escalate it to:
The investor's bank
The company's statutory auditor
The depository, and then SEBI through SCORES
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Unresolved complaints can be escalated to the depository and SEBI's SCORES platform.
Investor Services
Investors can protect their demat accounts against unauthorised debits by:
Signing a broad PoA with no limits
Sharing their OTPs with their broker
Not signing blank DIS and keeping the DIS booklet safe
Keeping the account dormant without any contact details
Blank signed DIS slips can be misused, so investors are advised to keep them safe.
vii: Which authority regulates financial services in International Financial Services Centres such as GIFT City?
IFSCA is the unified regulator for financial products and services in IFSCs.
The call money market deals in funds borrowed and lent for:
Call money is overnight borrowing and lending, mostly between banks.
Which of the following is a derivative product traded on Indian exchanges?
Options derive their value from an underlying stock or index.
Which of these is the main function of the secondary market?
Providing liquidity and price discovery for existing securities
Secondary markets let investors trade existing securities and discover prices.
Which statement about Treasury bills is correct?
They are short-term government securities issued at a discount
They are issued by private companies
They have maturities of more than ten years
T-bills are issued by the Government of India at a discount and redeemed at face value.
Government securities are issued by the RBI on behalf of the government through:
Private placement to retail investors only
The RBI conducts auctions to issue dated G-Secs and T-bills.
Market Participants in the Securities Market
Which of these is classified as a Qualified Institutional Buyer?
QIBs include mutual funds, FPIs (other than certain categories), banks and insurers.
Market Participants in the Securities Market
Which entity acts as the central counterparty to trades executed on a stock exchange?
The clearing corporation becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer.
Market Participants in the Securities Market
Which intermediary is an agent of a stock broker, approved by the exchange, who deals with clients on the broker's behalf?
Authorised persons are appointed by brokers with exchange approval to provide access to trading platforms.
Market Participants in the Securities Market
Which regulator administers the Companies Act and oversees company registration?
MCA, through Registrars of Companies, administers company law.
Market Participants in the Securities Market
A custodian in the securities market mainly serves:
Institutional investors such as FPIs and mutual funds, holding and servicing their securities
Custodians provide safekeeping, settlement and corporate action services to institutions.
Market Participants in the Securities Market
Which category of investor is a Hindu Undivided Family bidding for ₹5 lakh in an IPO?
Bids above ₹2 lakh by non-QIB investors fall under the non-institutional category.
Which is the correct order of the trade life cycle?
Order placement → order matching → trade confirmation → clearing → settlement
Order matching → settlement → order placement → clearing
Orders are placed and matched, confirmed, then cleared to determine obligations and finally settled.
Which function in a broking firm is mainly responsible for client acquisition and order entry?
The front office deals with clients, takes orders and executes trades.
Real-time monitoring of client exposures and limits in a broking firm is typically handled by the:
The middle office monitors risk and exposures against limits.
Preparing contract notes, maintaining client ledgers and reconciling funds and securities are functions of the:
The back office handles post-trade processing, accounting and reconciliation.
A client places an order to buy shares at ₹500 or lower. This is a:
A limit order sets the maximum buy price or minimum sell price.
An order that must execute immediately, with any unexecuted portion cancelled, is a(n):
IOC orders execute whatever is possible at once and cancel the rest.
Which of the following must a stock broker obtain from each client before trading?
Completed KYC, including PAN and the account opening documents
A bank guarantee from the client
KYC and documentation are mandatory before a client starts trading.
A sell order is triggered when the price falls to ₹450 and then placed as a limit order at ₹448. This is a:
The trigger price activates the order and the limit price caps the execution price.
VaR margin in the cash segment is designed to cover:
All possible losses under any scenario
The likely loss on a position over a given time horizon at a specified confidence level
Value at Risk estimates potential loss over a time horizon at a set confidence level.
Extreme Loss Margin (ELM) is collected to cover:
Losses beyond what VaR margin covers, in extreme market conditions
ELM covers tail risk that VaR does not capture.
A client buys 100 shares at ₹500. The closing price that day is ₹480. What is the mark-to-market loss?
A client buys shares worth ₹2,00,000. If the applicable VaR margin is 10% and ELM is 5%, what total upfront margin must the broker collect?
If a broker collects less margin from a client than required at the peak margin snapshots, the consequence is that:
No action is taken for retail clients
A penalty is levied for short collection of margin
The exchange refunds the trade value
Clearing corporations penalise short or non-collection of upfront margins.
The Core Settlement Guarantee Fund is maintained by:
The clearing corporation, to guarantee settlement of trades if a member defaults
SEBI, to fund its own expenses
The Core SGF absorbs losses from member defaults and supports the settlement guarantee.
Position limits and concentration limits in a broking firm mainly help to:
Prevent excessive exposure to a single client, security or segment
Limits contain concentration risk and potential losses.
A client's mark-to-market loss is not paid and the shortfall persists. A broker's risk team would most appropriately:
Ignore it until the client returns
Use another client's funds to cover the shortfall
Report the client to the income tax department
Square off positions as per the risk policy disclosed to the client
Brokers may liquidate positions under their risk policy; using other clients' money is prohibited.
Which bank function is linked to clearing corporations for the settlement of funds?
Clearing banks, through which members' funds pay-in and pay-out are made
Clearing members keep settlement accounts with designated clearing banks.
Determining which member must pay or receive how much money and securities after trading is part of:
Clearing computes the obligations of each member, which are then met during settlement.
Institutional trades that a custodian must confirm before they are settled carry a:
CP codes identify institutional trades settled through custodians.
In the clearing process, the clearing corporation interacts with depositories to:
Move securities for pay-in and pay-out
Depositories move securities from sellers and to buyers according to the clearing corporation's instructions.
The optional T+0 settlement cycle introduced by SEBI as a beta version:
Allows same-day settlement for a limited set of stocks, alongside the T+1 cycle
The beta T+0 cycle runs optionally for select scrips while T+1 continues.
Netting of obligations in clearing means:
Adding all trades together without offsetting
Offsetting a member's buy and sell positions in a security to arrive at a single net obligation
Settling each trade separately in gross
Netting reduces the number and value of transfers required in settlement.
Under T+1 settlement, a trade executed on a Friday (Monday being a working day) is settled on:
Settlement occurs on the next working day, which is Monday.
A trade is executed on Thursday and Friday is a trading holiday. Under T+1, settlement takes place on:
T+1 counts working days, so the next settlement day after Thursday is Monday.
If a selling member fails to deliver securities on the settlement day, the clearing corporation generally:
Conducts an auction to buy the shortfall securities, and closes out if the auction fails
Cancels the buyer's trade without compensation
Delivers shares from its own investment portfolio permanently
Asks SEBI to issue new shares
Shortages are met through an auction, and any unfilled shortfall is closed out at the prescribed price.
Funds pay-in by clearing members takes place through:
Their settlement accounts with clearing banks
Clearing banks debit and credit members' settlement accounts on the instructions of the clearing corporation.
When a stock goes ex-bonus, open derivative positions on that stock are:
Converted into cash at the previous closing price
Adjusted, for example in strike price and lot size, so that their value is maintained
Corporate action adjustments keep derivative contract values neutral to the event.
The pay-out of securities to a buying client under current norms is made:
Into the broker's own account for 30 days
Directly into the client's demat account by the clearing corporation
SEBI's direct payout framework credits securities straight to clients.
Determination of settlement obligations is based on:
Trades executed during the day and the netting rules of the clearing corporation
Obligations are computed from executed trades, netted by member and security.
SEBI's online platform for investors to file complaints against listed companies and intermediaries is:
SCORES allows online lodging and tracking of complaints.
If a dispute between an investor and a broker is not resolved through SCORES or direct engagement, the investor can use:
The Securities Appellate Tribunal directly as a first step
The consumer helpline of the telecom regulator
The Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) mechanism for conciliation and arbitration
SEBI's ODR framework lets investors escalate disputes to online conciliation and arbitration.
The Investor Protection Fund of a stock exchange is mainly used to:
Cover investors' market losses on investments
Compensate investors' eligible claims against brokers declared defaulters
IPF pays legitimate claims of investors when a broker defaults; it does not cover market losses.
Under SCORES, a registered intermediary must generally resolve a complaint within:
SEBI's revised SCORES framework requires entities to resolve complaints within 21 calendar days.
Which of the following is NOT a valid ground for a complaint against a stock broker?
A fall in the market price of shares the investor chose to buy
Non-receipt of funds after a sale
Market losses on the investor's own decisions are investment risk, not a service deficiency.
Under the Margin Trading Facility, a stock broker:
Buys shares for clients using other clients' funds
Funds part of a client's purchase of eligible securities, which are pledged as collateral
MTF lets brokers finance purchases of eligible stocks, with the purchased shares pledged to the broker.
The minimum investment required from a client for Portfolio Management Services is:
SEBI's PMS regulations set a minimum ticket size of ₹50 lakh.
Stock brokers can facilitate transactions in mutual fund units for clients through:
The exchange mutual fund platforms, such as NSE's and BSE's MF platforms
The RBI's Retail Direct portal only
Exchanges provide mutual fund transaction platforms that brokers use.
Internet Based Trading by a stock broker requires the broker to:
Obtain permission from the stock exchange and maintain adequate security and system controls
IBT needs exchange approval and must meet prescribed security and system standards.
